“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”
Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.
Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.
According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:
- 227,229 lives could potentially have been saved
- 158,138 complications could potentially have been avoided
“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.
“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.
“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”
Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:
- location
- transportation
- insurance
- financial challenges
Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.
“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.
“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”
Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:
- Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards recognize hospitals with outstanding clinical performance across 19 specialty care areas.
- Healthgrades Outpatient Awards honor national leaders in Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, and Outpatient Prostate Care.
- Healthgrades Specialty State Rankings identify the highest-performing hospitals across 19 specialties in 30 eligible states.
Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.
“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.
Specialty Excellence Awards and top hospitals
Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.
The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.
Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.
Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.
“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.
“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.
Healthgrades Outpatient Awards
Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.
Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.
From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.
“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.
“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.
To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.
“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.
Healthgrades Specialty State Rankings
State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.
Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.
The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.
State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.
The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.
These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.
With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.
Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.
The methodologies for each of the specialty awards can be found on the following pages:
For more information, Healthgrades’ Specialty Excellence Patient Advocate Center provides access to the information you need to make informed decisions about your care. This resource includes an overview of how Healthgrades picks award recipients, plus a list of the top U.S. hospitals for specialty care.

sources.title: Emerj — Healthcare AI: Artificial Intelligence at Quest Diagnostics – Two Use Cases
sources.text:
Quest Diagnostics reported $11 billion in net revenues and processed about 244 million test requisitions in 2025. The company serves roughly one in three U.S. adults each year and about half of U.S. physicians and hospitals. At this scale, even incremental improvements in laboratory and customer service workflows can affect substantial volumes of work.
Quest reported that its company-wide Invigorate program met its 3% annual cost savings and productivity improvement target in 2025, reflecting the combined results of the program’s initiatives, including AI and automation.
In June 2024, it completed the acquisition of select PathAI Diagnostics lab assets to advance AI and digital pathology. In March 2025, it announced a collaboration with Google Cloud to improve data analytics and explore generative AI across research, customer experience, and operations, with several of those applications still under exploration.
This article examines two internal AI use cases at Quest Diagnostics:
- Supporting Pap test slide review with AI-assisted digital cytology: AI selects images from digitized Pap test slides for review by cytologists and pathologists.
- Supporting customer service calls and emails with AI: A virtual agent handles routine logistics calls, while AI tools help route incoming emails and help representatives find answers faster.
We begin by examining how Quest applies AI-assisted digital cytology to high-volume cervical cancer screening, where specialist time is scarce.
Supporting Pap Test Slide Review with AI-assisted Digital Cytology
Pap test slide review depends on cytologists and pathologists, making specialist staffing a factor in how many slides a lab can review.
The American Society for Clinical Pathology’s 2024 vacancy survey found that the vacancy rate in U.S. cytology departments fell from 13.2% in 2022 to 11.6% in 2024. In the 2022 survey, respondents reported that filling cytology staff positions took more than 12 months.
For labs evaluating the workflow, the question is whether existing staff can review more slides and deliver results sooner while maintaining or improving screening performance.
On Quest’s April 2026 earnings call, CEO Jim Davis estimated that 60% to 70% of the company’s AI and automation efforts were focused on its labs. He described how Quest looks for opportunities to use AI by asking whether what specialists examine under a microscope can be captured in digital images that algorithms can analyze.
Quest uses the Hologic Genius Digital Diagnostics System in cervical cancer screening. Quest describes the system as using an AI algorithm with digital imaging to help identify precancerous and cancerous cells.
According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) review, it works in three connected steps:
- Imaging: In conventional review, specialists examine the glass slide under a microscope. With Genius, a digital imager scans each stained Pap test slide.
- AI-assisted selection: A deep learning model selects images of cells and cell clusters for the review gallery and provides a cell count to help specialists assess whether the sample is adequate.
- Professional review: Cytologists and pathologists review the full gallery on high-resolution stations and are responsible for the diagnosis.
Hologic describes secure remote sharing of cases, a capability of the digital imaging infrastructure rather than of the AI itself, which can help labs distribute review work across locations.
In its 2024 annual report, Quest described how it uses AI to separate specimens with no evidence of microbial growth so medical scientists can focus on specimens more likely to indicate disease.
In its 2023 Investor Day presentation, Quest reported that it had reduced the microbiology workflow from eight steps to two, improved turnaround time for negative cultures by 40%, and reduced the full-time staffing required for the workflow by about 40%. The figures reflect the combined effects of automation and AI.
In a four-site study of 1,960 evaluable slides, sensitivity for high-grade lesions or worse was 81.5% with the Genius system, compared with 74.0% for manual review.
At the same threshold, specificity fell from 97.2% with manual review to 94.8% with Genius, a statistically significant difference. The digital system detected more high-grade abnormalities, but the lower specificity can also mean more slides without high-grade abnormalities are flagged for further review.
A retrospective study at ProPath, a Dallas pathology laboratory, compared Pap test workflows before and after the lab introduced Hologic’s Genius Digital Diagnostics System. Average daily review volumes were similar, while cases reviewed per cytologist per day rose from 74.5 to 94.7 and the average number of cytologists working per day fell from 10.4 to 8.1. The time from specimen accession to final sign-out also fell across diagnostic categories.
Hologic funded the study and employed one co-author. The study covered one lab and included about eight months of data after implementation. The authors did not use biopsy data to confirm the increase in disease detection, and the before-and-after comparison could not isolate AI’s contribution to the workflow changes.
In its February prepared remarks, Quest said it had implemented the Genius system at two laboratories and planned to expand it to several more that year. On the July earnings call, Davis said Quest had recently installed the system at two more locations, following implementations at about half a dozen sites over the previous year.
At its 2025 Investor Day, Quest projected that implementing Genius would improve resource productivity by more than 40%. The February and July updates described rollout progress and gave no measured productivity result.
Supporting Customer Service Calls and Emails with AI
Quest’s customer service operation connects the physician offices, hospitals, and patients it serves with its labs and courier network. Much of that work is routine: physician offices, for example, schedule courier pickups by calling a central line and saying “specimen pickup” to reach dispatch. Requests like these are the kind of high-volume, repeatable contact a service operation at Quest’s scale has to absorb.
Quest’s contact centers handled 13.2 million interactions in 2024, up from 12.2 million in 2023. Phone calls accounted for 71% of interactions in 2024. In its 2025 Investor Day presentation, Quest showed that calls per 100 requisitions fell from 6.2 in 2022 to 5.5 in 2023 and held at 5.5 in 2024, an 11% reduction from the 2022 baseline.
On Quest’s Q3 2026 earnings call, Davis estimated that wage inflation would be 3% to 4% in 2026. He said wage inflation puts at least $120 million in cost pressure on Quest each year and that the company uses its Invigorate program to help offset that pressure.
Across its filings and earnings calls, Quest has described three AI applications in use:
- Answer retrieval for representatives: In its 2024 annual report, Quest said it is broadening its use of AI in customer service to help representatives access answers more quickly.
- A virtual AI agent for logistics calls: Davis said the agent handles routine logistics calls. Quest’s 2025 Investor Day describes voice recognition software that interacts with clients to schedule routine pickups, which it says reduces client wait times and frees staff for higher-priority requests. Quest has not said whether this is the same tool as the virtual agent, though both target routine logistics calls.
- AI triage for customer service email: Davis described customer service agents using AI to triage and route customer emails to speed responses.
Quest describes three changes to its customer service workflow:
- A virtual agent handles routine logistics calls.
- AI helps triage and route incoming emails.
- Representatives use AI to find answers more quickly.
On impact, Quest has given two headline figures, both self-reported. Davis said the virtual AI agent has reduced routine logistics calls by “up to” 50%, a best case rather than an average. He reported a 40% productivity gain in Q1 2026 among customer service agents who used AI to triage emails, without a published methodology or comparison group.
Beyond those figures, Quest has not named the vendors or models behind these tools, or disclosed which call types the agent covers, adoption levels, volumes, costs, or AI’s share of Invigorate savings. Customer service AI has appeared in its reporting from 2023 through 2026, which shows sustained attention rather than proven scale.
Quest’s examples suggest a simple sorting rule for leaders deciding where AI belongs in a contact center:
- Routine, repeatable spoken requests: Route to a virtual agent first, as Quest has done with logistics calls.
- Unstructured written requests: Use AI to triage and route, and keep a person on the resolution, as Quest has done with email.
- Live requests that reach a representative: Keep the person on the call and use AI to find answers faster, as Quest describes in its annual report.
- Measurement: Track calls per 100 requisitions to account for changes in testing volume. Measure agent productivity against a defined baseline and, where feasible, compare it with that of a similar group working without the AI tools.
This analysis examines the following lessons enterprise leaders can draw from Quest Diagnostics’ AI adoption:
- Check what the digital input preserves: Before choosing an algorithm, confirm that the digital record captures the details specialists need to make a decision.
- Set the boundary for automation: Define which cases AI can route or complete, which findings specialists must interpret, and when to escalate uncertain cases.
- Measure each tool against its own baseline: Track changes in throughput, quality, and cost for the workflow the tool affects, and report those results separately from program-wide savings.

Abstract

Background:
Antithrombotic stewardship is critical for reducing preventable harm from inappropriate anticoagulant prescribing. Electronic health record (EHR)–embedded clinical decision support (CDS) alerts can prevent prescribing errors at the point of care, but their real-world effectiveness is variable and often limited by alert fatigue and poor workflow integration. Whether augmenting interruptive medication alerts with just‑in‑time access to clinical pharmacists improves prescriber response remains unclear.


Objective:
This study aimed to (1) compare the effectiveness of synchronous, interruptive direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) prescribing alerts with and without an embedded clinical pharmacist referral option for correcting inappropriate new prescriptions within 7 days, and (2) evaluate the system‑level impact of implementing synchronous DOAC alerts on inappropriate prescribing over time.


Methods:
We conducted a prescriber‑level randomized comparative effectiveness trial within a large US academic health system. Prescribers who placed an inappropriate ambulatory apixaban or rivaroxaban order were randomized to receive an interruptive EHR alert either with or without an embedded clinical pharmacist referral link. The primary outcome was any change to the prescription within 7 days. In parallel, a system‑level interrupted time series analysis examined weekly proportions of inappropriate DOAC prescriptions (secondary outcomes) from 24 months before through 29 months after alert implementation. Exploratory outcomes included adverse events within 30 days and alert implementation metrics.


Results:
Among 2082 prescribers writing DOAC prescriptions during the study period, 300 (14.4%) triggered at least one inappropriate prescription and were randomized; after prespecified exclusions, 758 alerts across 286 prescribers were analyzed. Overall, 28.9% (219/758) of alerts led to a prescription change within 7 days. The proportion of alerts leading to a prescription change did not differ between alerts with and without pharmacist referral (difference 1 percentage point [95% CI −7 to 9]). The system‑wide proportion of inappropriate DOAC prescriptions exhibited a significant downward preimplementation trend (−0.04 percentage points per week [95% CI −0.06 to −0.02]), followed by an immediate 3.5‑percentage‑point absolute reduction at alert launch (to 9.7%), with no subsequent slope change. Adverse events within 30 days were uncommon and similar across arms.


Conclusions:
Adding an embedded pharmacist referral option to an interruptive DOAC prescribing alert did not increase short‑term prescription changes. However, the implementation of synchronous, user-centered alerts was associated with a system-level reduction in inappropriate DOAC prescribing. These findings support a complementary digital stewardship model in which high‑value, point‑of‑order alerts prevent routine prescribing errors, while clinical pharmacists focus on complex and longitudinal medication management.

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05351749; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05351749

Introduction

Inappropriately prescribed anticoagulant medications are the leading cause of adverse drug events, with dosing errors and unrecognized drug-drug interactions contributing to preventable patient harm and health care resource use [1-3]. Health systems are increasingly investing in antithrombotic stewardship as a core patient-safety strategy to standardize prescribing, monitor therapy, and mitigate risk [4-6]. Population health approaches, including pharmacist-led dashboards, have reduced inappropriate direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) medication prescriptions and even reduced adverse clinical event rates [7-10]. However, they are labor-intensive and typically only identify prescribing errors after an order has been placed.

Computerized clinical decision support (CDS) tools, including medication alerts, hold promise for preventing errors at the point of prescribing. However, the real-world impact of these interruptive alerts has been mixed, often limited by insufficient or inactionable information, workflow disruptions, and alert fatigue [11]. User-centered design, incorporating human-factors principles, has been proposed to improve alert acceptance and impact, yet prospective evaluations embedded in routine care remain scarce [12,13].

Because many prescribing-based CDS tools are ignored or overridden and contribute to alert fatigue, one component of antithrombotic stewardship that remains untested is the opportunity to connect prescribers with clinical pharmacists—either to collaborate on decision-making or to fully offload decision-making [14]. This collaboration, facilitated by CDS tools, could improve the utility of prescribing alerts while also better integrating pharmacists into just-in-time, point-of-care decision-making. However, no studies have yet examined the potential effectiveness of this type of CDS tool in antithrombotic prescribing, particularly when compared with more traditional best-practice alerts.

To better inform how health care systems might design prescribing CDS alerts to improve evidence-based prescribing, we developed and implemented a set of electronic health record (EHR)–embedded DOAC medication alerts, grounded in user-centered design principles. As part of this rollout, we aimed to evaluate 2 questions. First, using prescriber-level randomization, we compared whether adding a direct, in-line referral process for engaging clinical pharmacists in prescribing decisions increased the rate of prescribers changing inappropriate DOAC prescriptions beyond what alerts alone achieved. Second, in parallel, we used an interruptive time series analysis to prospectively evaluate the system-wide impact of implementing synchronous medication alerts on the system-level proportion of DOAC prescriptions that were inappropriate.



Methods
Study Overview and Setting

As part of a larger program testing several strategies to reduce inappropriate DOAC prescribing and improve evidence-based prescribing [15], we conducted a 2-arm randomized comparative-effectiveness trial of 2 DOAC medication alerts. Specifically, we randomized eligible prescribers to receive 1 of 2 types of CDS interruptive alerts whenever they ordered a DOAC prescription that did not follow the package label instructions. This study focused on inappropriate ambulatory DOAC prescriptions that occurred at the time of ordering within the EHR (ie, new DOAC prescriptions) rather than those that developed longitudinally for already existing prescriptions (eg, related to a change in renal function); the latter were addressed in a companion trial and the results of that study have been previously published [16].

Within a large, quaternary care health system in the midwestern United States, we initially implemented a series of medication alerts for patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) on August 1, 2022, and conducted a pilot study to examine the acceptability, accuracy, and feasibility of these alerts [13]. Subsequently, on April 12, 2023, we further implemented alerts for patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE). Prescribers were randomized (and thus entered the study) upon ordering their first inappropriate DOAC prescription for either AF or VTE after alerts were launched for patients managed in the ambulatory setting. This study includes both the pilot study and expanded trial periods, with continued clinician enrollment until December 15, 2024, the end of the trial. Prior to the commencement of the randomized trial, all inappropriate DOAC prescriptions in the health system were captured on a population health DOAC Dashboard. Updated HIPAA privacy law sets rules for sharing health data with apps

HHS Office for Civil Rights Director Paula Stannard said she’s “convinced” the rule will enable health data sharing and better care coordination.

Published Nov. 17, 2026
Jill Hughes
Reporter
Share
License
Add us on Google
Exterior view of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services headquarters in Washington, D.C., on July 3, 2017. Alamy
Listen to the article
6 min

LAS VEGAS — The HHS Office for Civil Rights finalized modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule on Monday, aimed at increasing patients’ access to their own medical records. The rule, initially proposed in 2020, contains a slew of substantive updates to the foundational health data privacy rule that seek to reduce administrative friction and encourage health data sharing.

The final rule slashes the timeframe for providers to respond to patient record requests in half, from 30 calendar days to 15. It also enables providers to share more health information with certain third parties, like social workers, in a play to enhance care coordination. And in line with the Trump administration’s enthusiasm for patient access to digital health tools, patients will also be able to obtain copies of their records via health apps.

“I know that lots of people have been looking forward to this rule. Some believe that it should have been done much earlier,” OCR Director Paula Stannard said during a session at the HLTH 2026 conference.

“But we are convinced that this will provide individuals with faster access to health information while at the same time facilitating health information interoperability, enhancing care coordination, reducing regulatory burden and protecting the privacy of individual health information as we seek to improve the healthcare system by making information more interoperable.”

The rule will go into effect 60 days after it’s published on the federal register, which is set to happen on Thursday. Healthcare providers, payers and their business associates will be expected to comply around July 10, or roughly six months after the effective date.

The HHS estimates that the rule will result in $784 million in new costs within a year of implementation, but that those upfront costs will be offset by net cost savings of $703 million annually in years two through five.

The department says the majority of the savings will come from eliminating the requirement that healthcare providers obtain a signed acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of privacy practices, which the HHS says currently costs providers significant time and money.

HIPAA revamp targets patient records access, app sharing

When HIPAA was enacted in 1996, the commercial internet was in its infancy and electronic health records were not yet widely adopted. The regulation initially set out to help people transfer health insurance when they switched jobs and to standardize health information, but it later evolved to set standards for privacy and security in the sector.

Since the HIPAA Privacy Rule was tacked onto the law in 2003, it has served as the preeminent federal regulation for safeguarding the privacy and confidentiality of protected health information transmitted by providers, payers and their business associates. It sets strict parameters for how and when healthcare organizations can use or disclose PHI and gives patients the right to request access to their records, mandating that they receive them in a timely manner.

Giving patients access to their medical records has been a priority under President Donald Trump’s OCR, and remains one of the top complaints the agency receives. During his first administration, the OCR launched an enforcement initiative to discipline providers that fail to provide patients timely access to their records, and the agency has cracked down on 55 organizations over the last seven years.

The new rule smooths the road for providers to share health records with patients by adding definitions for “personal health application” and “electronic health record,” two terms that HIPAA had never explicitly defined before. 

Before, providers faced significant uncertainty about permitting health apps to access patient records because it was unclear whether patient data would be at risk once records were sent to an app that isn’t covered by HIPAA.

Now, the rule’s tightened language gives providers a clearer path to send health data to apps. It plainly states that if a patient asks for their records to be sent to a health app that meets the agency’s definitions, they must do so.

A personal health application, according to the final rule, is an app used by an individual to access their own health information, even if that information is drawn from multiple sources. The app must be controlled by that individual, rather than an organization or another person.

Commenters on the proposed rule were divided on whether the personal health app definition should be broader, covering more platforms and use cases, or narrower, to only include apps that met strict security and privacy standards. The HHS largely finalized the provision as proposed, without adding additional security limits, taking a broader approach.

An electronic health record, in the eyes of HIPAA, is now formally defined as an electronic record of “health-related information on an individual that is created, gathered, managed, and consulted by authorized health care clinicians and staff,” the rule states.

Among the rule’s many other elements is a provision that prohibits entities from imposing “unreasonable” identity verification requirements on an individual wanting to access their health records, such as requiring a patient to appear in person when there’s a method for remote verification available. Organizations must also start posting the cost of obtaining medical records on their websites. 

Days before the rule was finalized, a coalition of healthcare executives wrote a letter to HHS asking it not to finalize the rule on the grounds that certain provisions would make it difficult for providers to confirm whether a third-party application has been authorized by a patient to receive their PHI. They also raised concerns about the move to loosen the verification requirements.

Despite the security concerns, the rule was finalized largely as proposed. 

The HIPAA Security Rule, the privacy rule’s sister regulation that sets standards for the protection of electronic health information, is also due for a long-anticipated update next summer.

‘Selling and marketing snake oil’: The debate over compounded GLP-1s

Experts have serious concerns with telehealth companies building lucrative businesses off the back of compounded weight loss drugs. The FDA is cracking down.

Published Nov. 17, 2026
Rebecca Pifer Parduhn
Senior Reporter
Share
License
Add us on Google
An assortment of weight loss and diabetic drugs sit on a table in New South Wales, Australia, in May 2024. Getty Images
Listen to the article
7 min

LAS VEGAS — Many telehealth companies have made a name off compounded GLP-1s, touting the benefits of building custom formulations from scratch. But critics are increasingly worried about safety and efficacy — and the downstream ramifications of allowing companies to peddle unregulated drugs as America’s growing interest in wellness and biohacking drives more consumers to unproven therapies.

A massive compounding industry has cropped up around GLP-1s, with companies offering to deliver the popular weight loss drugs directly to consumers’ doors for a few hundred dollars per month. That’s attracted millions of Americans, turned off by the greater than $1,000 list price for brand-name GLP-1s like Zepbound or Wegovy and unwilling to wait years until cheaper generic versions of the medications to become available.

Proponents of the model argue it increases access, drives prices down and helps patients who may need unique versions of the medication. But it comes with a significant catch: compounded drugs aren’t reviewed by the Food and Drug Administration for safety or effectiveness before they’re sold, raising concerns about preparation mistakes, contamination and other issues.

Regulators generally don’t allow pharmacies to compound — or combine and mix ingredients to create a new product — commercially available drugs like GLP-1s.

But the FDA allowed compounding pharmacies to produce the medications for a brief window starting in 2022, during a shortage of GLP-1s. Restrictions went back into effect in late 2024 and early 2025. Yet many compounding pharmacies have continued formulating new versions of the drugs, rejigging ingredients or delivery methods so they can claim the resulting products differ from brand-name medication.

“To me, all of those [compounding use cases] feel like stealing from pharma manufacturers. And you can say whatever you like about the ethics of stealing from pharma manufacturers, but you’re taking something that they have a patent on and claiming that you have this legal permissibility to copy it. And it’s tenuous, that legal permissability,” Michael Botta, the co-founder and president of Sesame, a cash-pay marketplace for care, said in an interview at HLTH.

But compounding is good for patients, including groups like women who may benefit from unique dosing, Kathleen Jordan, the chief medical officer of virtual care provider Midi Health, said during a panel on Sunday at the HLTH conference in Las Vegas. Midi offers compounded GLP-1s.

Sign up

Some patients may need smaller or more customized dosages of the drugs, according to Jessica Duncan, the chief medical officer of Ivim Health. Ivim is a telehealth platform that provides access to compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide, the active ingredient in GLP-1s.

“We see that patients who, especially on semaglutide, who have slower titration tend to stay on therapy, tend to have improved side effects, and tend to have the same efficacy,” Duncan said during the panel.

But many experts are leery about the compounded medications, pointing to risks like dosing errors or fraudulent labels. Adverse events associated with compounded GLP-1s have continued to rise, with the FDA reporting almost 1,000 reports associated with compounded semaglutide alone as of this May.

“The pharmacists I work with are appalled,” said Dr. Amy Compton-Phillips, chief medical officer of CVS. “The drug substance that comes into the compounders have less of the FDA approval and less of the oversight around them. It can be done in a high-quality way. But you just don’t quite have the same seal that what you’re injecting directly into your body is pure and unadulterated.”

Proponents argue that similar guardrails exist for compounded medications as branded drugs. Licensed clinicians should always be prescribing the drugs through a licensed pharmacy with appropriate board oversight, according to Dr. Mohit Joshipura, the chief medical officer of OpenLoop Health.

Patients who receive compounded medications should need a unique version of the drug. And prescribers should be honest about the risks associated with compounded GLP-1s, and follow-up about side effects and efficacy, Joshipura said.

OpenLoop, a company that helps third parties stand up telehealth businesses and connects them with compounding pharmacies, was sued earlier this year for marketing and selling compounded GLP-1s as a safe and effective alternative to FDA-approved medication.

The FDA has sent dozens of warning letters to telehealth companies for making false or misleading statements about compounded GLP-1s, including representing the drugs as comparable with brand-name products.

One company that received a letter, MEDVI, is on track for $1.8 billion in sales this year, the New York Times reported in April.

This spring, the FDA proposed permanently excluding semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide — another GLP-1 class drug — from the ingredients that major compounding pharmacies are legally allowed to use. If finalized, the change would bring large-scale GLP-1 compounding to a halt, according to law firm ArentFox Schiff.

But proponents of compounding drugs argue it’s too late to put the genie back into the bottle. Of the 27 million adults who are estimated to have used a GLP-1 last year, at least 23% used a compounded version, according to researchers with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Another 9% said they were unsure whether their GLP-1 was compounded or not.

That’s at least six million Americans who would lose access to their medications if compounding ground to a halt, Joshipura said. Some of those patients would switch to a brand-name medication, but many others would stop taking GLP-1s entirely, losing the health benefits and likely regaining any lost weight — or seek out the drugs from shadier players.

If compounded GLP-1 therapies went away, more than 85% of Ivim’s patients said they would consider going to other sources online that have no provider oversight and no standards, according to Duncan.

“That number keeps me up at night,” she said.

“I think we’re past the question of whether compounding should exist. It’s very much a question of how can this co-exist alongside the FDA-approved medications,” Joshipura said.

Sesame sold compounded GLP-1s during the shortage, but stopped when it was declared over. To Botta, the argument that compounded drugs are necessary to meet patients’ unique needs is unconvincing, given GLP-1s are already available in multiple doses.

He also worries that telehealth companies that have built lucrative businesses off compounded GLP-1s could be opening the floodgates to other unproven therapies.

“Over the last 24 months we saw a bunch of companies pop up that built a business around promoting on TikTok or promoting through influencers the idea of taking compounded GLP-1s. And now those folks are saying ’Oh, I already have compounded GLP-1s. Well, what’s the next thing we’re going to sell people through this channel? And that’s becoming peptides. It’s becoming [testosterone replacement therapy],” Botta said.

Direct-to-consumer pathways are needed to ensure access to care amid physician shortages and steep prices, he added. But some companies are taking advantage.

“There’s a long history in the United States of people selling and marketing snake oil,” Botta said. “I worry that some of these folks are turning to places that are now trying to sell them trash.”

sources.title: WHO News: WHO guidance helps detect iron deficiency and protect brain development
sources.text:
Detecting iron deficiency early during pregnancy and in young children is crucial. Iron deficiency in children under two years of age can have significant and irreversible effects on brain development. This can lead to negative consequences on learning and school performance later in life. Cognitive development of a child can also be affected if a mother is iron deficient during her last trimester of pregnancy. New World Health Organization guidelines on the use of ferritin concentrations to assess iron status in individuals and populations will help health workers to detect iron deficiency early and avoid the most severe impacts.
WHO shows how to best measure ferritin, an indicator of iron stores, to help determine iron deficiency or overload. Ferritin is a protein which can be found in small amounts circulating in a person’s blood. Ferritin levels are low in iron-deficient individuals and high in iron-loaded individuals. Accurate measurements of this protein, along with clinical and laboratory evaluation, can guide the appropriate interventions in both individual patients and at a population level.
“Reducing anemia is one of the components of our efforts to eradicate all forms of malnutrition. However, progress has been limited and we still have 614 million women and 280 million children globally who suffer from it,” said Dr Francesco Branca, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO. “Iron deficiency is a major determinant of anemia and measuring ferritin, a key biomarker of iron metabolism, will help us better target and evaluate our action to fight anemia”
Iron is an essential element with important functions such as oxygen transport, DNA synthesis and muscle metabolism. Iron deficiency is the main cause of anaemia, which is the most prevalent nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting 33% of non-pregnant women, 40% of pregnant women, and 42% of children worldwide.
In adults, iron deficiency can also have negative effects including fatigue, impaired physical performance and decreased work productivity, as well as impacting social activities. Iron deficiency occurs mainly when the requirements of iron increase during rapid periods of growth and development such as in early childhood, adolescence and pregnancy, but it can occur at other stages in life. In pregnant women, iron deficiency can cause anaemia, reduced birth weight and reduced gestation periods.
The new guidelines also cover the early detection of iron overload. Iron overload (accumulation of iron in the body) is generally the result of disorders such as hereditary haemochromatosis, thalassaemia, repeated blood transfusions or other conditions that affect iron absorption or regulation and can also lead to deterioration of a person’s health if left untreated.
Improved knowledge about the prevalence and distribution of iron deficiency and risk of iron overload in the population helps countries to decide on appropriate interventions, and to monitor and evaluate the impact and safety of public health programmes. For example, nutritional iron deficiency can be commonly found in populations that also have infectious diseases. The adequate evaluation of iron status in countries with infectious disorders can help countries to put in place adequate health policies.
The WHO guidelines aim to help WHO Member States and their partners to make evidence-informed decisions on appropriate actions in their efforts to lower iron deficiency and improve the health and quality of life of individuals and populations.

sources.text: National Safe Staffing Ratios | National Nurses United Skip to main content Safe Staffing Ratios NNU’s proposal for minimum, mandated, nurse-to-patient staffing ratios protect our patients’ right to nursing care. We know that every patient deserves a single standard of high-quality care. Safe staffing ratios, coupled with nurses’ powerful voice of advocacy secured in collective bargaining, protect our patients from complications that arise from missed care such as medical errors, health care disparities, infections, and so much more. Read more » Nurse Staffing Standards for Hospital Patient Safety and Quality Care Act fact sheet Read our fact sheet on legislation that would protect patients and improve health care by setting mandated, minimum, registered nurse-to-patient staffing ratios. There is No Nurse Shortage There is a nurse retention crisis due to the hospital industry’s systematic failure to invest in safe, quality, human-to-human patient care. Hospital management has created a staffing crisis. About safe staffing ratios Image The science of ratios  Decades of studies have shown that more nurses equate to lives saved and fewer complications. Researchers have been focusing on what exactly is the mediating link between increasing RN staffing and improved outcomes. Image Learning from the California experience  In 1999, the registered nurses of the California Nurses Association successfully sponsored and lobbied the California Legislature to pass A.B. 394, the historic bill that made minimum, specific numerical staffing ratios the golden standard in the Golden State. Image What does the California ratios law actually require?  The CNA-sponsored safe staffing law has multiple provisions designed to remedy unsafe staffing in acute-care facilities. California’s safe staffing standards are based on individual patient acuity, of which the RN ratios is the minimum. We need your help to get the Nurse Staffing Standards for Hospital Patient Safety and Quality Care Act passed to improve working conditions for nurses and to protect patients. Take action by urging your elected officials to support this critical legislation. Take action Learn more Reports Image Protecting Our Front Line: Ending the Shortage of Good Nursing Jobs and the Industry-created Unsafe Staffing Crisis  In this report, National Nurses United describes how the hospital industry has driven registered nurses from the bedside. Image RN Staffing Ratios: A Necessary Solution to the Patient Safety Crisis in U.S. Hospitals  NNU stands ready to help you bring ratios to your state. Read our booklet to learn more. Image RN Staffing Ratios Whitepaper  Registered nurse staffing levels that facilitate safe, competent, therapeutic, and effective care are vital to the safety of patients in U.S. hospitals. Research reveals that these ratios are associated with lower mortality, lower nurse burnout, and better nurse retention. Videos Join our fight for safe staffing Safe RN ratios have been proven to improve the quality of care and nurse recruitment and retention in California hospitals. California and beyond California is the only state in the country that puts a legal limit on the number of patients a nurse can be made to care for at one time. National Nurses United fights for safe staffing ratios in our union contracts and for federal legislation for safe staffing ratios.  All staffing ratios videos Articles National safe staffing bill reintroduced in Congress National Nurses United applauded the reintroduction of federal legislation to mandate minimum registered nurse-to-patient ratios in every hospital across the country. The bill is sponsored by Rep. Jan Schakowsky and new Senate sponsors, Sen. Alex Padilla and Sen. Jeff Merkley. July 11, 2025 Nurses march nationwide for safe staffing, patient protections against A.I. Thousands of registered nurse members of National Nurses United (NNU) held actions, including marches, protests, and rallies, on Jan. 16 to demand the hospital industry ensure safe staffing levels and patient safeguards amidst the rapid introduction of artificial intelligence technologies. April 21, 2025 VA nurses across country fight for safe staffing, protest hiring freeze Registered nurses who work at Veterans Affairs (VA) hospitals around the country, from New York to Ohio to North Carolina to Florida, held a national week of action in August. The nurses are calling on the VA to lift what is in effect a hiring freeze that has contributed to more than tens of thousands of vacancies across the health system, including thousands of RN positions. September 23, 2024 Press releases UCI Health Irvine nurses to hold rally protesting unsafe staffing, elimination of night-shift ICU support Registered nurses at UCI Health Irvine in Irvine, California, will hold a rally and picket on Wednesday, October 28, to highlight their increasing concerns about unsafe working conditions and the removal of certified nursing assistants (CNAs) from ICU night shifts. October 23, 2026 Monterey nurses to rally for patient safety Registered nurses at the Community Hospital of Monterey Peninsula (CHOMP), in Monterey, California will hold a rally on Monday, October 26 to highlight their patient safety concerns, including short-staffing and ongoing workplace violence issues. October 23, 2026 New report finds cost-cutting at MedStar Franklin Square puts patient care in jeopardy A new report, “The Cost of Cutting Care: How MedStar Is Failing Franklin Square Nurses and Patients”, released by National Nurses United, finds chronic registered nurse (RN) understaffing by MedStar Franklin Square Medical Center in Baltimore, Md., puts patient care at risk and leads to numerous poor outcomes as measured by U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. October 9, 2026 California Nurses Association registered nurses celebrate their victory in implementing long-awaited safe staffing ratios for state’s acute psychiatric hospitals California nurses are celebrating today, June 1, the historic implementation of long-awaited safe nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in the state’s acute psychiatric hospitals (APH) that should dramatically improve the care behavioral health patients receive and that RNs can provide.
